A Winter Crossing to Skerry Holm

Forty miles of open water in January, a borrowed ketch, and one very patient weather window.

CS
Callum Strand10 November 2026 · 9 min read

Nobody crosses to Skerry Holm in January for the scenery, although the scenery is extraordinary. You cross because the island is there, because the ferry has stopped for the season, and because a friend with a ketch and more courage than sense has asked whether you are free on Saturday.

The weather window was eleven hours wide. We left Port Avelin in the dark at six, with a northwesterly that the forecast promised would ease by noon and back into the south by evening. For once, the forecast was right. The sea was long and grey and orderly, the kind of sea that lifts a boat rather than throws it, and by mid-morning we had the island’s cliffs on the bow.

What surprises you about a winter crossing is the light. The sun never climbs much above the horizon, so the whole day is a long, low golden hour. The water is the color of slate, then pewter, then for a few minutes after noon an astonishing pale green. We tied up at Holm Quay at half past two, ate soup in the harbor café with the ferry crew, and were back in Port Avelin before the wind turned. ■
